# Model Comparison, Partial F Tests, and ANOVA {#sec-model-comparison}

In this chapter, we study the ANOVA decomposition for linear regression, the overall significance test, and the comparison of nested models. These ideas connect the geometry of least squares with the inferential tools developed in [Chapter 2 — Least Squares Estimation](02_LSE.qmd) and [Chapter 3 — Distribution Theory of OLS and Inference](03_OLS_inference.qmd).

> **Learning Objectives**
>
> By the end of this chapter, students should be able to:
>
> -   define the total, regression, and error sums of squares;
> -   explain the ANOVA decomposition in regression with an intercept;
> -   interpret the degrees of freedom associated with SST, SSR, and SSE;
> -   perform the overall $F$ test for regression;
> -   compare nested linear models using extra sums of squares;
> -   interpret ANOVA tables produced by statistical software.

**Reading**

Recommended reading for this chapter:

-   Seber and Lee:
    -   sections on analysis of variance in regression
    -   sums of squares and decomposition of variability
    -   tests for nested models
-   Montgomery, Peck, and Vining:
    -   sections on the ANOVA table
    -   overall model significance
    -   partial and sequential sums of squares

::: {.callout-note title="Motivation: does measuring tree height add useful information?"}

Suppose a forestry team wants to estimate timber volume before felling a tree. Diameter is already available; measuring height requires additional effort. Does height contribute information beyond diameter?

The real `trees` dataset in R lets us explore this question with measurements on 31 felled black cherry trees. Consider three candidate mean models:

| Model | Information used | Mean volume |
|---|---|---|
| $M_0$ | No tree measurements | $\beta_0$ |
| $M_1$ | Diameter | $\beta_0+\beta_1\,\mathrm{Diameter}$ |
| $M_2$ | Diameter and height | $\beta_0+\beta_1\,\mathrm{Diameter}+\beta_2\,\mathrm{Height}$ |

**Discuss before calculating:** Which comparison answers whether height adds information? Why is choosing the smallest training SSE insufficient? Keep these questions in mind; the optional data example below returns to them with fitted models.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Recap of the Linear Model"}

Recall the normal linear model

$$
\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \sim N_n(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_n).
$$

When $\mathbf{X}$ has full column rank, the ordinary least squares estimator is

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
=
(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{Y},
$$

and the fitted values are

$$
\hat{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.
$$

The residual vector is

$$
\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{Y} - \hat{\mathbf{Y}}.
$$

From [Chapter 2 — Least Squares Estimation](02_LSE.qmd), we know that $\hat{\mathbf{Y}}$ and $\mathbf{e}$ are orthogonal. From [Chapter 3 — Distribution Theory of OLS and Inference](03_OLS_inference.qmd), we know that this leads to useful distributional results for inference. In this chapter, we organize these ideas into the ANOVA framework.

:::

**Vector notation.** Following the convention used in this course, $\mathbf a=(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ denotes a column vector, while $\mathbf a^\top=(a_1\;a_2\;a_3)$ denotes a row vector. Commas distinguish the column-vector tuple; spaces separate entries of the row vector.

## Total, Explained, and Unexplained Variation

A central question in regression is: How much of the variation in the response can be explained by the model? To answer this, we decompose the total variation in $\mathbf{Y}$ into:

-   variation explained by regression;
-   variation left unexplained by the model.

When the model includes an intercept, this decomposition takes a particularly simple and important form.

::: {#def-regression-sums-of-squares}

## Regression Sums of Squares

For an OLS fit with an intercept, let $\bar Y=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$, $\hat{\mathbf Y}=\mathbf X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$, and $\mathbf e=\mathbf Y-\hat{\mathbf Y}$. Define the **total**, **error**, and **regression sums of squares** by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{SST}&=\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y)^2
=\|\mathbf Y-\bar Y\mathbf 1\|^2,\\
\mathrm{SSE}&=\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\hat Y_i)^2
=\mathbf e^\top\mathbf e,\\
\mathrm{SSR}&=\sum_{i=1}^n(\hat Y_i-\bar Y)^2
=\|\hat{\mathbf Y}-\bar Y\mathbf 1\|^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

SST measures variation around the sample mean; SSE measures deviations from the fitted model; SSR measures how much the fitted values vary around the sample mean. These are definitions. Their additive relationship below follows from OLS orthogonality and the inclusion of an intercept.

::: {.callout-important title="A deviation may be negative; a sum of squares cannot"}

The subtraction inside each definition produces a **signed deviation**, which can be negative, zero, or positive. We then **square that deviation** and add the squared values. Thus

$$
\mathrm{SST}\geq0,\qquad \mathrm{SSR}\geq0,\qquad \mathrm{SSE}\geq0.
$$

For example, $y_i-\hat y_i=-0.6$ is a residual, while its contribution to SSE is $(-0.6)^2=0.36$. A negative residual is not a negative SSE. Also, $(a-b)^2$ is not $a^2-b^2$. Reversing the direction of a deviation changes its sign but leaves its square unchanged.

:::


::: {#thm-anova-decomposition}

## ANOVA Decomposition with an Intercept

For an ordinary least squares fit whose design matrix contains an intercept,

$$
\mathrm{SST}=\mathrm{SSR}+\mathrm{SSE}.
$$

The centered fitted vector $\hat{\mathbf Y}-\bar Y\mathbf 1$ is orthogonal to the residual vector $\mathbf e$. Thus total variation around the sample mean splits into explained variation and residual variation. This geometric identity does not require normal errors.

:::

**Why the Decomposition Holds**

The key reason is orthogonality. We can write

$$
\mathbf{Y} - \bar{Y}\mathbf{1}
=
(\hat{\mathbf{Y}} - \bar{Y}\mathbf{1})
+
(\mathbf{Y} - \hat{\mathbf{Y}}).
$$

That is,

$$
\mathbf{Y} - \bar{Y}\mathbf{1}
=
(\hat{\mathbf{Y}} - \bar{Y}\mathbf{1}) + \mathbf{e}.
$$

Because the model contains an intercept, the vector $\bar{Y}\mathbf{1}$ lies in the column space of $\mathbf{X}$. Hence both $\hat{\mathbf{Y}}$ and $\bar{Y}\mathbf{1}$ lie in the model space, so their difference also lies in the model space. Since the residual vector $\mathbf{e}$ is orthogonal to the model space, we have

$$
(\hat{\mathbf{Y}} - \bar{Y}\mathbf{1})^\top \mathbf{e} = 0.
$$

Therefore, by the Pythagorean theorem,

$$
\|\mathbf{Y} - \bar{Y}\mathbf{1}\|^2
=
\|\hat{\mathbf{Y}} - \bar{Y}\mathbf{1}\|^2
+
\|\mathbf{e}\|^2,
$$

which is exactly

$$
\mathrm{SST} = \mathrm{SSR} + \mathrm{SSE}.
$$

::: {#exr-intercept-anova-discussion}

## In-Class Discussion: Why Does the Intercept Matter?

Why does the usual centered decomposition $\mathrm{SST}=\mathrm{SSR}+\mathrm{SSE}$ require the model space to contain the constant vector? Which step could fail without an intercept? Does this identity require normal errors?

:::

::: {#sol-intercept-anova-discussion}

With an intercept, $\mathbf 1$ and therefore $\bar Y\mathbf 1$ belong to the model space. Thus the centered fitted vector $\hat{\mathbf Y}-\bar Y\mathbf 1$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf e$, and the cross term vanishes when its squared norm is expanded. Without a constant vector in the model space, $\sum_i e_i$ need not be zero, so the cross term $\mathbf e^\top(\hat{\mathbf Y}-\bar Y\mathbf 1)=-\bar Y\sum_i e_i$ need not vanish. The identity follows from OLS geometry, not normality.

:::

::: {#exr-identify-anova-deviations}

## In Class: One Observation, Three Deviations

For one observation, $y_i=1$, $\hat y_i=1.2$, and $\bar y=3$. In one minute, identify the total, explained, and residual deviations. Does the squared total deviation equal the sum of the other two squared deviations for this observation?

:::

::: {#sol-identify-anova-deviations}

The deviations are $y_i-\bar y=-2$, $\hat y_i-\bar y=-1.8$, and $y_i-\hat y_i=-0.2$. They add as signed deviations: $-2=-1.8-0.2$. Their squares do not add: $4\ne3.24+0.04$. The ANOVA identity holds after summing over all observations because the fitted and residual vectors are orthogonal; it is not a point-by-point identity for squared deviations.

:::

**Degrees of Freedom**

The ANOVA decomposition is accompanied by a decomposition of degrees of freedom. When the model includes an intercept and $\mathbf{X}$ has rank $p$, we have:

-   total degrees of freedom: $n-1$;
-   regression degrees of freedom: $p-1$;
-   error degrees of freedom: $n-p$.

Thus,

$$
n-1 = (p-1) + (n-p).
$$

These match the sum of squares decomposition:

$$
\mathrm{SST} = \mathrm{SSR} + \mathrm{SSE}.
$$

::: {#def-regression-mean-squares}

## Regression and Error Mean Squares

A **mean square** is a sum of squares divided by its associated degrees of freedom. For a full-rank regression design with an intercept and $1<p<n$, define

$$
\mathrm{MSR}=\frac{\mathrm{SSR}}{p-1},\qquad
\mathrm{MSE}=\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n-p}.
$$

Here $p$ includes the intercept coefficient.

:::

Dividing by degrees of freedom accounts for the different dimensions contributing to each sum of squares. Under the linear-model moment assumptions from [Chapter 3 — Distribution Theory of OLS and Inference](03_OLS_inference.qmd), MSE is an unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2$. MSR estimates the same noise level under the overall null hypothesis, which motivates their ratio.

## The Overall F Test

A major inferential question is whether the regression model provides any explanatory power beyond the intercept-only model. Suppose the model includes an intercept and $p-1$ additional predictors. The null hypothesis is

$$
H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \cdots = \beta_{p-1} = 0,
$$

where $\beta_0$ is the intercept and $p$ counts all regression coefficients. Equivalently, under $H_0$, the mean response does not depend on the predictors. The alternative is that at least one non-intercept coefficient is nonzero.

::: {#thm-overall-f}

## Overall F Test

Under the normal linear model with a fixed, full-rank design containing an intercept and $1<p<n$, the null hypothesis that all non-intercept coefficients are zero gives

$$
F=\frac{\mathrm{SSR}/(p-1)}{\mathrm{SSE}/(n-p)}
=\frac{\mathrm{MSR}}{\mathrm{MSE}}
\sim F_{p-1,n-p}.
$$

Large values provide evidence against the intercept-only mean model. Exact finite-sample inference requires the normal, common-variance error assumptions; the sum-of-squares identity alone does not supply this distribution.

:::

**Interpretation of the Overall F Test**

The numerator measures explained variation per regression degree of freedom. The denominator measures unexplained variation per residual degree of freedom. So the $F$ statistic compares:

-   how much signal the model explains;
-   how much noise remains in the residuals.

If the predictors have no effect, then both quantities should be of similar size, and the ratio should not be unusually large. If the predictors explain substantial variation, then the numerator should be much larger than the denominator.

::: {#exr-overall-f-question}

## In Class: What Does an Overall Rejection Mean?

An intercept model with two predictors is fitted to $n=25$ observations using a full-rank design. Write the overall null hypothesis and the F reference degrees of freedom under the normal linear model. How does this joint test differ from the individual t tests? If it rejects, must both individual slope tests also reject?

:::

::: {#sol-overall-f-question}

Here $p=3$, so $H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=0$ and the reference distribution is $F_{2,22}$. Rejection gives evidence that the two slopes are not jointly zero. It does not show that both are nonzero, and it does not require either individual test to reject at the same level. Each individual t test asks whether one slope is zero while retaining the other predictor; the overall F test asks whether both slopes are jointly zero. These are different questions, especially when predictors are correlated.

:::

**Relationship to the Intercept-Only Model**

The overall $F$ test compares two models:

-   the reduced model: intercept only;
-   the full model: intercept plus predictors.

Thus the ANOVA decomposition provides the basis for formal model comparison. This leads naturally to the idea of nested models.

## Nested Models

Before comparing models, we need to say what their regression parameters mean.

::: {#def-regression-parameter-meaning}

## Regression Coefficients and the Mean Response

For fixed predictor values, consider the additive model

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\beta_2x_{i2}+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad \mathbb E(\varepsilon_i)=0.
$$

The **mean response function** is $\mu(x_1,x_2)=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2$. If predictors are random, read this as a conditional mean, with $\mathbb E(\varepsilon\mid x_1,x_2)=0$.

| Parameter | Interpretation in this additive model |
|:----------:|:--------------------------------------------------|
| $\beta_0$ | The intercept: mean response when both $x_1=0$ and $x_2=0$. |
| $\beta_1$ | Difference in mean response for a one-unit increase in $x_1$, holding $x_2$ fixed. |
| $\beta_2$ | Difference in mean response for a one-unit increase in $x_2$, holding $x_1$ fixed. |

For example,

$$
\mu(x_1+h,x_2)-\mu(x_1,x_2)=h\beta_1.
$$

Thus a positive $\beta_1$ means a higher mean response at larger $x_1$ when $x_2$ is fixed; a negative value means a lower mean. Its units are **response units per unit of $x_1$**. A zero coefficient means no change in this model's mean as $x_1$ varies with $x_2$ fixed; it does not rule out an unadjusted association between $x_1$ and $Y$.

:::

**Parameter, estimate, and observation.** The coefficients $\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2$ are unknown model parameters. The fitted coefficients $\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_2$ are estimates calculated from a sample and vary across samples. Substituting them gives a fitted mean $\hat\mu$. An individual observed response also contains its error term, so a slope does not prescribe the exact difference between two observations. These mean comparisons do not by themselves establish a causal effect.

::: {#exm-regression-parameter-meaning}

## Read a Fitted Equation in Its Units

For the trees introduced earlier in this chapter, a fitted equation is

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Volume}}
=-57.988+0.339\,\mathrm{Height}+4.708\,\mathrm{Diameter}.
$$

Volume is in cubic feet, height in feet, and diameter in inches.

- $\hat\beta_{\mathrm{Height}}=0.339$: at the **same diameter**, trees one foot apart in height differ by an estimated 0.339 cubic feet in mean volume. A five-foot difference corresponds to $5(0.339)=1.695$ cubic feet, using the rounded slope.
- $\hat\beta_{\mathrm{Diameter}}=4.708$: at the **same height**, a one-inch diameter difference corresponds to an estimated 4.708-cubic-foot difference in mean volume.
- $\hat\beta_0=-57.988$: the fitted mean at height zero and diameter zero. Those values are outside the observed data, so this intercept is an extrapolated baseline, not a useful prediction for an actual tree.

The larger numerical diameter coefficient does not by itself make diameter the more important predictor: the predictors have different units and ranges, and the two coefficients describe different comparisons. The fitted coefficients also do not tell us their own uncertainty; that requires the standard errors and inference from Chapter 3.

:::

We can now ask how these interpretations change when a predictor is added.

::: {#def-nested-linear-models}

## Nested Linear Models

For the same response vector and observations, let the reduced and full models have mean spaces $\mathcal C(\mathbf X_R)$ and $\mathcal C(\mathbf X_F)$. The models are **nested** when

$$
\mathcal C(\mathbf X_R)\subseteq\mathcal C(\mathbf X_F).
$$

Thus every mean vector allowed by the reduced model is also allowed by the full model. A strict comparison requires ranks $p_R<p_F$; adding columns that are linear combinations of existing columns does not enlarge the mean space.

:::

::: {#exm-nested-regression-models}

## Adding a Predictor

Use different parameter symbols to keep the two candidate mean models distinct:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_R(x_1)&=\alpha_0+\alpha_1x_1,\\
\mu_F(x_1,x_2)&=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2.
\end{aligned}
$$

| Coefficient | Mean comparison described by its model |
|:----------:|:--------------------------------------------------|
| $\alpha_1$ | A one-unit difference in $x_1$, without adjusting for $x_2$. |
| $\beta_1$ | A one-unit difference in $x_1$, holding $x_2$ fixed. |
| $\beta_2$ | A one-unit difference in $x_2$, holding $x_1$ fixed. |

The reduced intercept is the mean at $x_1=0$ under the reduced model; the full intercept is the mean at $x_1=x_2=0$ under the full model. Each interpretation depends on the specified mean function and on whether its baseline is supported by the data.

Setting $\beta_2=0$ recovers the reduced mean function, with $\alpha_0=\beta_0$ and $\alpha_1=\beta_1$ **under that restriction**. If the $x_2$ column is not in the span of the intercept and $x_1$, the full model adds one degree of freedom.

When we fit the two models separately, OLS re-estimates every free coefficient. Nestedness therefore does **not** require $\hat\alpha_1=\hat\beta_1$. Even if the reduced model is true, fitting the unrestricted full model can give different estimates in a finite sample. [Chapter 5](05.qmd#exm-ch5-tree-adjustment) illustrates this with the same height measurements before and after adjustment for diameter.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Interpret the restriction in the full model"}

For the models above, the partial F comparison tests $H_0:\beta_2=0$: does $x_2$ contribute to the mean after accounting for $x_1$? It does not directly test equality of the two fitted $x_1$ coefficients. A change in the size, sign, or p-value of the $x_1$ coefficient can accompany the change in adjustment; compare the scientific questions before comparing printed numbers.

:::

::: {#exr-nested-parameter-interpretation}

## In Class: Which Parameter Is Being Tested?

Compare `Volume ~ Height` with `Volume ~ Height + Diameter` on the same trees. Which null hypothesis does their partial F test address?

A. The two fitted height coefficients are equal.

B. The diameter coefficient in the full model is zero, after accounting for height.

C. The height coefficient in the full model is zero, after accounting for diameter.

:::

::: {#sol-nested-parameter-interpretation}

**B.** Diameter is the added predictor. Statement C would instead compare `Volume ~ Diameter` with `Volume ~ Diameter + Height`. Neither comparison is a direct test that the height estimates from two different models are equal.

:::

::: {#def-extra-sum-of-squares}

## Extra Sum of Squares

For nested models fitted by OLS to the same response and observations, define the **extra sum of squares** for the full model relative to the reduced model as

$$
\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{extra}}=\mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_F.
$$

Its associated degrees of freedom are $p_F-p_R$, where $p_R$ and $p_F$ are the design-matrix ranks.

:::

::: {#exr-nested-sse-discussion}

## In-Class Discussion: Can the Larger Model Fit Worse?

Why must $\mathrm{SSE}_F\le\mathrm{SSE}_R$ when nested models are fitted by OLS to the same observations? Must the inequality be strict whenever a genuinely new predictor direction is added?

:::

::: {#sol-nested-sse-discussion}

Every fitted mean vector allowed by the reduced model is also available to the full model. Minimizing the same residual sum of squares over this larger set cannot give a larger minimum. Equality is possible even if the model space grows: for the observed response, the added directions may provide no further reduction in residual variation. Thus greater flexibility guarantees a weak improvement in training fit, not a strictly positive improvement or a useful predictor.

:::

A positive extra sum of squares alone is not evidence against the reduced model: the F test scales that improvement by its degrees of freedom and the estimated noise variance.

::: {#thm-partial-f}

## Partial F Test for Nested Normal Linear Models

Fit both models to the **same response and the same observations**. Suppose their fixed design matrices have nested column spaces, with ranks $p_R<p_F<n$, and the full model has independent $N(0,\sigma^2)$ errors. Under the null hypothesis that the mean belongs to the reduced model,

$$
F=\frac{(\mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_F)/(p_F-p_R)}{\mathrm{SSE}_F/(n-p_F)}
\sim F_{p_F-p_R,n-p_F}.
$$

Large values give evidence against the reduced mean model. The numerator measures improvement per added degree of freedom; the denominator estimates the unexplained variance under the full model.

:::

The [appendix at the end of this chapter](#sec-f-test-appendix) derives $\mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_F$ geometrically and shows how @thm-overall-f is the special case of @thm-partial-f in which the reduced model contains only an intercept.

::: {.callout-important title="Compare the models, not just the printed p-values"}

Different missing-value patterns can cause two R fits to use different observations. Construct a common analysis dataset before comparing them. For one added coefficient, the partial F statistic equals the square of its two-sided t-test statistic from the full model.

:::

::: {#exr-partial-f-short-calculation}

## In Class: A Better Fit, but Enough Improvement?

Two nested models use the same $n=30$ observations. The reduced model has rank $p_R=2$ and $\mathrm{SSE}_R=90$; the full model has rank $p_F=4$ and $\mathrm{SSE}_F=78$. Compute the extra sum of squares, its degrees of freedom, the full-model MSE, and the partial F statistic. Does a reduction in SSE by itself justify rejecting the reduced model?

:::

::: {#sol-partial-f-short-calculation}

The improvement is $90-78=12$ on $4-2=2$ degrees of freedom. The full-model MSE is $78/(30-4)=3$, so $F=(12/2)/3=2$. Under the normal-model null, compare this with $F_{2,26}$; the upper-tail p-value is about $0.156$. The improvement is insufficient for rejection at the 5% level. More flexibility always weakly reduces training SSE, including when the added coefficients are zero.

:::

**Connection with General Linear Hypotheses**

Nested column-space models correspond to linear restrictions on the full-model coefficients. More generally, [Chapter 3 — Distribution Theory of OLS and Inference](03_OLS_inference.qmd) allows a specified affine restriction of the form

$$
H_0: \mathbf{C}\boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{d}.
$$

So the ANOVA comparison of nested models is another way of expressing the general $F$ test from [Chapter 3 — Distribution Theory of OLS and Inference](03_OLS_inference.qmd). In practice, this is one of the most common uses of regression ANOVA tables.

::: {#def-sequential-partial-sums-of-squares}

## Sequential and Partial Sums of Squares

For a term in a specified regression model, both quantities are extra sums of squares from a nested comparison on the same observations:

- **Sequential sum of squares:** the reduction in SSE when the term is added after the preceding terms in a specified order.
- **Partial sum of squares:** the increase in SSE when the specified term is removed from a full model while the other specified terms are retained.

:::

When predictors are correlated, sequential sums of squares can depend on their order. Partial sums of squares answer a comparison conditional on the terms retained in the reduced model. With interactions or rank deficiency, state the exact restriction and respect model hierarchy rather than relying only on a Type I, II, or III label.

::: {#def-coefficient-of-determination}

## Coefficient of Determination

For an OLS fit with an intercept and $\mathrm{SST}>0$, the **coefficient of determination** is

$$
R^2=\frac{\mathrm{SSR}}{\mathrm{SST}}
=1-\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\mathrm{SST}}.
$$

:::

By the ANOVA decomposition, $R^2$ lies between 0 and 1 and measures the proportion of centered variation explained by the fitted model. If every observed response is identical, $\mathrm{SST}=0$ and this ratio is undefined.

**Interpretation of R Squared**

-   If $R^2$ is close to 1, the model explains a large proportion of the variation in the response.
-   If $R^2$ is close to 0, the model explains little of the variation.

However, $R^2$ alone does not guarantee that the model is appropriate. A high $R^2$ does not ensure that assumptions are satisfied, and a low $R^2$ does not necessarily imply the model is useless.

::: {#def-adjusted-r-squared}

## Adjusted Coefficient of Determination

For an OLS fit with an intercept, $\mathrm{SST}>0$, and design rank $p<n$, define the **adjusted coefficient of determination** as

$$
R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}
=1-\frac{\mathrm{SSE}/(n-p)}{\mathrm{SST}/(n-1)}.
$$

:::

Ordinary $R^2$ cannot decrease when the model space is enlarged on the same data. Adjusted $R^2$ accounts for the loss of residual degrees of freedom and can decrease or become negative. It compares residual mean square with the sample variance of the response; it is not a literal proportion of explained variation or an estimate of out-of-sample predictive performance.

::: {#exm-anova-by-hand}

## A Small ANOVA Calculation

For the column vectors $\mathbf x=(0,1,2,3)$ and $\mathbf y=(1,3,3,5)$, the fitted line is $\hat y=1.2+1.2x$. Therefore $\hat{\mathbf y}=(1.2,2.4,3.6,4.8)$, $\mathbf e=(-0.2,0.6,-0.6,0.2)$, and $\bar y=3$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{SST}&=(1-3)^2+(3-3)^2+(3-3)^2+(5-3)^2=8,\\
\mathrm{SSE}&=(-0.2)^2+0.6^2+(-0.6)^2+0.2^2=0.8,\\
\mathrm{SSR}&=\mathrm{SST}-\mathrm{SSE}=8-0.8=7.2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $n=4$ and $p=2$, so the regression, residual, and total degrees of freedom are 1, 2, and 3, respectively.

| Source | Sum of squares | df | Mean square | F |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Regression | 7.2 | 1 | 7.2 | 18 |
| Error | 0.8 | 2 | 0.4 | |
| Total | 8.0 | 3 | | |

The model has $R^2=7.2/8=0.9$, yet the F-test p-value is $P(F_{1,2}\ge18)\approx0.0513$. With only two residual degrees of freedom, a high training $R^2$ does not automatically give evidence at the 5% significance level.

:::

::: {#exr-r-squared-versus-adjustment}

## In Class: Can Two Fit Summaries Disagree?

For the same $n=10$ observations with $\mathrm{SST}=100$, an intercept model has rank 2 and SSE 20. Adding a predictor whose column is linearly independent of the existing columns increases the rank to 3 and reduces SSE to 19. Compute $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$ for both fits. Did the one-unit reduction in SSE improve both summaries? Why can relying on $R^2$ alone be misleading?

:::

::: {#sol-r-squared-versus-adjustment}

Ordinary $R^2$ increases from $1-20/100=0.80$ to $1-19/100=0.81$. Adjusted $R^2$ decreases from $1-(20/8)/(100/9)=0.775$ to $1-(19/7)/(100/9)\approx0.756$. The extra predictor reduces SSE but increases residual mean square, from $2.5$ to about $2.714$. Training $R^2$ cannot decrease when the model space grows, even when the new term only fits noise. A high $R^2$ also does not establish a correct mean function, appropriate error assumptions, or causality. Neither summary alone establishes better prediction on new observations.

:::

**ANOVA Table Structure**

A standard regression ANOVA table has the following structure:

| Source     | Sum of Squares | Degrees of Freedom | Mean Square | F       |
|------------|----------------|--------------------|-------------|---------|
| Regression | SSR            | $p-1$              | MSR         | MSR/MSE |
| Error      | SSE            | $n-p$              | MSE         |         |
| Total      | SST            | $n-1$              |             |         |

Students should learn to move fluently between:

-   formulas;
-   geometric interpretation;
-   software output.

## R Demonstration

**Fit a simple regression model**

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
            theme(legend.position = "bottom",
              panel.grid.minor = element_blank()))

x <- c(0, 1, 2, 3)
y <- c(1, 3, 3, 5)

fit <- lm(y ~ x)
summary(fit)
```

**Obtain the ANOVA table**

```{r}
anova(fit)
```

**Verify sums of squares manually**

```{r}
ybar <- mean(y)
yhat <- fitted(fit)
e <- resid(fit)

SST <- sum((y - ybar)^2)
SSE <- sum(e^2)
SSR <- sum((yhat - ybar)^2)

c(SST = SST, SSR = SSR, SSE = SSE)
SST - SSR - SSE
```

**From deviations to sums of squares.** @fig-anova-variation separates three operations: **subtract, square, then add**. Each column is one of the four observations. Read downward from a signed difference to its nonnegative squared contribution, then add across the row to obtain SS. The minus signs in the first row describe deviations; the boxed totals are the sums of squares.

```{r}
#| label: fig-anova-variation
#| cache: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "How to compute SST, SSR, and SSE from the same four observations. The first row in each panel contains signed deviations, the second contains their squares, and the box at the right contains the sum of those squares. Negative deviations become positive contributions when squared. The resulting sums are SST = 8.00, SSR = 7.20, and SSE = 0.80; none is negative."
#| fig-alt: "Three arithmetic panels show subtract, square, add. Total deviations minus 2, 0, 0, 2 become squares 4, 0, 0, 4, summing to SST 8. Explained deviations minus 1.8, minus 0.6, 0.6, 1.8 become squares 3.24, 0.36, 0.36, 3.24, summing to SSR 7.2. Residuals minus 0.2, 0.6, minus 0.6, 0.2 become squares 0.04, 0.36, 0.36, 0.04, summing to SSE 0.8."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-pos: "H"
source("illustrations/anova-sums-and-geometry.R")
draw_anova_sums(y, yhat)
```

**Adding deviations is different from adding their squares.** For these residuals,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_i e_i&=-0.2+0.6-0.6+0.2=0,\\
\mathrm{SSE}=\sum_i e_i^2&=0.04+0.36+0.36+0.04=0.80.
\end{aligned}
$$

The signed residuals sum to zero because the OLS model includes an intercept. Their squared values do not cancel. Here all three SS values are strictly positive; in general an SS can equal zero when every corresponding deviation is zero.

:::: {#anova-xy-companion}

**The same deviations in the $x,y$ plane.** Each point represents one of the four observations. The three panels use identical axes to show total, explained, and residual deviations. Squaring and adding the colored vertical differences gives the SS values in @fig-anova-variation.

```{r}
#| label: anova-xy-companion
#| cache: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Three vertically stacked panels with identical axes. Panel A connects the mean 3 to observed values, with differences minus 2, 0, 0, and 2. Panel B connects the mean to fitted values, with differences minus 1.8, minus 0.6, 0.6, and 1.8. Panel C connects fitted to observed values, with residuals minus 0.2, 0.6, minus 0.6, and 0.2. Each endpoint type has a distinct shape, and every difference is labeled."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 7.4
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-pos: "H"
library(ggplot2)
variation <- rbind(
  data.frame(x, y, yhat, start = ybar, end = y, component = "Total"),
  data.frame(x, y, yhat, start = ybar, end = yhat, component = "Explained"),
  data.frame(x, y, yhat, start = yhat, end = y, component = "Residual"))
variation$component <- factor(variation$component,
                              levels = c("Total", "Explained", "Residual"))
variation$difference <- variation$end - variation$start
variation$label <- ifelse(abs(variation$difference) < 1e-10, "0.0",
                         sprintf("%+.1f", variation$difference))
endpoints <- rbind(
  transform(variation, value = start,
    kind = ifelse(component == "Residual", "Fitted", "Mean")),
  transform(variation, value = end,
    kind = ifelse(component == "Explained", "Fitted", "Observed")))
endpoints$kind <- factor(endpoints$kind,
                         levels = c("Observed", "Fitted", "Mean"))
panel_labels <- c(
  Total = sprintf("A  TOTAL: observed - mean     |     SST = %.1f", SST),
  Explained = sprintf("B  EXPLAINED: fitted - mean     |     SSR = %.1f", SSR),
  Residual = sprintf("C  RESIDUAL: observed - fitted     |     SSE = %.1f", SSE))

ggplot(variation, aes(x)) +
  geom_hline(data = subset(variation, component != "Residual"),
             aes(yintercept = ybar), colour = "grey60", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_abline(data = subset(variation, component != "Total"),
              aes(intercept = coef(fit)[1], slope = coef(fit)[2]),
              colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = x, y = start, yend = end, colour = component),
               linewidth = 1.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = endpoints, aes(y = value, shape = kind, fill = kind),
             colour = "grey20", size = 2.8, stroke = 0.9) +
  geom_label(aes(x = x + 0.14, y = (start + end) / 2,
                label = label, colour = component),
             hjust = 0, fontface = "bold", size = 3.8, fill = "white",
             linewidth = 0, label.padding = grid::unit(0.07, "lines"),
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(Observed = 16, Fitted = 21, Mean = 22)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Observed = "black", Fitted = "white",
                                Mean = "grey75")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Total = "#0072B2", Explained = "#00805A",
                                  Residual = "#C34700")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = x) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:5) +
  facet_wrap(~ component, ncol = 1,
              labeller = as_labeller(panel_labels)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.25, 3.7), ylim = c(0.5, 5.5)) +
  labs(x = "Predictor x (same four observations in every panel)",
        y = "Response value", shape = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0, size = 10.5),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey95", colour = NA),
        panel.spacing.y = grid::unit(0.8, "lines"))
```

::: {.figure-caption}

Companion $x,y$ view for @fig-anova-variation. Filled circles are observed responses, open circles are fitted values, and squares mark the sample mean. The dashed line is the mean; the thin gray line is the fitted regression. Colored vertical segments show total (blue), explained (green), or residual (orange) deviations; their labels are signed differences, not sums of squares. Squaring and adding within each panel gives SST = 8.0, SSR = 7.2, and SSE = 0.8.

:::

::::

For example, at $x=1$, the observed value equals the mean, so the **total deviation is zero**. Nevertheless, the explained deviation is $2.4-3=-0.6$ and the residual is $3-2.4=+0.6$. They cancel as signed differences: $0=-0.6+0.6$. Their squares do not cancel. Only after summing across all four observations do we obtain $8.0=7.2+0.8$.

**Compute R squared manually**

```{r}
R2 <- SSR / SST
R2
summary(fit)$r.squared
summary(fit)$adj.r.squared
pf(18, df1 = 1, df2 = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

**Compare nested models**

```{r}
dat <- data.frame(
  y = c(4, 5, 7, 10, 8, 12, 13, 14),
  x1 = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8),
  x2 = c(2, 1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 6, 5)
)

fit_reduced <- lm(y ~ x1, data = dat)
fit_full <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dat)

anova(fit_reduced, fit_full)
```

**Inspect the two fitted models**

```{r}
summary(fit_reduced)
summary(fit_full)
```

**Interpretation of Software Output**

For a fitted model in R:

-   `anova(fit)` gives sequential sums of squares in the order terms enter a single model;
-   `anova(fit_reduced, fit_full)` compares nested models;
-   `summary(fit)` reports the overall $F$ statistic, $R^2$, and adjusted $R^2$.

Students should understand that these outputs are not separate topics. They are all built from the same least squares geometry and distribution theory.

::: {#exm-timber-volume}

## Optional Real-Data Example: Is Tree Height Useful Beyond Diameter?

Return to the forestry question. R's `trees` data contain timber volume in cubic feet, height in feet, and a variable named `Girth` that is actually **diameter in inches**, measured 4 feet 6 inches above the ground. We rename it `Diameter` to avoid that labeling trap. Each row represents one of 31 felled black cherry trees. See the [official dataset documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/trees.html) for the source and measurement definitions.

**State the question first.** Comparing $M_0$ with $M_2$ asks whether diameter and height together improve on a constant mean. Comparing $M_1$ with $M_2$ asks whether height contributes after adjusting for diameter. For the second question, $H_0:\beta_{\mathrm{Height}}=0$. These are distinct questions even though both use an F test.

```{r}
tree_dat <- datasets::trees
tree_dat$Diameter <- tree_dat$Girth
tree_dat <- tree_dat[, c("Volume", "Diameter", "Height")]
stopifnot(!anyNA(tree_dat))
fit_tree0 <- lm(Volume ~ 1, data = tree_dat)
fit_tree_d <- lm(Volume ~ Diameter, data = tree_dat)
fit_tree_dh <- lm(Volume ~ Diameter + Height, data = tree_dat)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Model = c("Constant mean", "Diameter", "Diameter + height"),
  Rank = c(fit_tree0$rank, fit_tree_d$rank, fit_tree_dh$rank),
  SSE = c(deviance(fit_tree0), deviance(fit_tree_d),
          deviance(fit_tree_dh))), digits = 2)
anova(fit_tree_d, fit_tree_dh)
```

**Read the comparison.** The SSE drops from about $524.30$ to $421.92$. The added term uses one degree of freedom, and the full model has $31-3=28$ residual degrees of freedom. Thus

$$
F=\frac{(524.30-421.92)/1}{421.92/28}\approx6.79,
\qquad p\approx0.0145.
$$

Under the stated normal, common-variance error model, this provides evidence against a zero height coefficient after accounting for diameter. It is not the overall test of both slopes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tree-model-comparison
#| cache: false
#| fig-cap: "The same 31 trees under two mean models. The legend identifies black filled dots as observed volumes, blue open circles as fitted volumes, and orange vertical segments as residuals (observed minus fitted). Each segment connects the observation and prediction for one tree. Adding height reduces the sum of squared residual lengths, but the F test asks whether that improvement is large relative to the estimated noise."
#| fig-alt: "Two scatterplots compare diameter only with diameter plus height. A shared legend below both panels shows a black filled dot for observed volume, a blue open circle for fitted volume, and an orange line for the residual, observed minus fitted. Orange vertical segments connect each tree's observed and fitted values."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
library(ggplot2)
tree_comparison <- rbind(
  transform(tree_dat, prediction = fitted(fit_tree_d),
    model = "Diameter only"),
  transform(tree_dat, prediction = fitted(fit_tree_dh),
    model = "Diameter + height"))
tree_comparison$model <- factor(tree_comparison$model,
                                levels = c("Diameter only",
                                  "Diameter + height"))
ggplot(tree_comparison, aes(Diameter, Volume)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = Diameter, yend = prediction, colour = "Residual"),
    linewidth = 0.65, show.legend = TRUE) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = "Observed"), shape = 16, size = 1.8,
    show.legend = TRUE) +
  geom_point(aes(y = prediction, colour = "Fitted"), shape = 1, size = 2,
    show.legend = TRUE) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(Observed = "black", Fitted = "#0072B2", Residual = "#B84400"),
    breaks = c("Observed", "Fitted", "Residual"),
    labels = c("Observed volume", "Fitted volume",
               "Residual (observed minus fitted)")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE,
    override.aes = list(shape = c(16, 1, NA), linetype = c(0, 0, 1),
                        size = 2.8, linewidth = 0.8))) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Diameter (inches)", y = "Timber volume (cubic feet)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 11),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.3, "lines"),
        legend.key.height = grid::unit(1, "lines"))
```

**Check your understanding.** Why use 28 rather than 29 in the variance estimate? What would change if some trees had missing heights? The denominator comes from the full model. With missing heights, first form one common dataset and refit both models on it; comparing fits on different observations confounds the added predictor with a changed sample.

**What this example does not settle.** These are observational measurements, so the comparison is not a causal effect of making a tree taller. A statistically significant height term also does not decide whether measuring height is worth its cost or how much it helps predict new trees. Those decisions require practical error tolerances and validation. Inspect residuals and the mean function before using the raw-scale linear model operationally; transformations and model assessment appear later in the course.

:::

## Summary

In this chapter, we developed the ANOVA framework for linear regression. We defined:

$$
\mathrm{SST}, \qquad \mathrm{SSR}, \qquad \mathrm{SSE},
$$

and showed that, with an intercept,

$$
\mathrm{SST} = \mathrm{SSR} + \mathrm{SSE}.
$$

This decomposition led to:

-   the ANOVA table;
-   the overall $F$ test for regression;
-   the comparison of nested models through extra sums of squares;
-   the interpretation of $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$.

## Practice Problems

**Conceptual**

1.  Explain the meaning of SST, SSR, and SSE in words.
2.  Explain why the regression degrees of freedom are $p-1$ when the model includes an intercept.
3.  Explain the difference between the overall $F$ test and a test for a single coefficient.

**Computational**

Suppose a regression model with intercept has:

-   $n=20$,
-   $p=4$,
-   $\mathrm{SST}=100$,
-   $\mathrm{SSE}=40$.

Compute:

1.  $\mathrm{SSR}$,
2.  the degrees of freedom for regression and error,
3.  $\mathrm{MSR}$,
4.  $\mathrm{MSE}$,
5.  the overall $F$ statistic,
6.  $R^2$.

**Nested Model Problem**

A reduced model has $\mathrm{SSE}_R = 120$ with $p_R = 3$, and a full model has $\mathrm{SSE}_F = 90$ with $p_F = 5$. If $n=30$, compute the nested-model $F$ statistic.

**Suggested Take home exercise**

Complete the following tasks:

-   prove the decomposition $\mathrm{SST}=\mathrm{SSR}+\mathrm{SSE}$ when the model includes an intercept;
-   derive the overall $F$ statistic from the ANOVA decomposition;
-   fit a regression model in R and reproduce the ANOVA table by hand;
-   compare two nested models using an extra sum of squares test;
-   interpret both $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$ for a chosen dataset.

## Appendix: From the SSE Difference to the Overall F Test {#sec-f-test-appendix .unnumbered}

@thm-overall-f is the intercept-only special case of @thm-partial-f: the extra sum of squares $\mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_F$ then equals $\mathrm{SSR}$.

### A geometric picture of the extra sum of squares {.unnumbered}

Each vertex in @fig-nested-ss-geometry represents a vector of $n$ values. The green edge joins the reduced and full fitted vectors; its **squared length** is $\mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_F$.

For an intercept-only reduced model, $\hat{\mathbf Y}_R=(\bar Y,\ldots,\bar Y)^\top=\bar Y\,\mathbf1_n$, where $\mathbf1_n$ is the all-ones vector. Panel B uses the same four observations as @fig-anova-variation, with $\bar Y=3$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-nested-ss-geometry
#| cache: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: 'Squared lengths for nested OLS fits. Panel B uses the data in @fig-anova-variation: $\mathrm{SSE}_R=\mathrm{SST}=8$, $\mathrm{SSE}_F=\mathrm{SSE}=0.8$, and the green squared length is $\mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_F=\mathrm{SSR}=7.2$. The diagrams are schematic, not to scale.'
#| fig-alt: "Two right triangles with vertices for the reduced fitted vector, full fitted vector, and observed vector. Panel A gives the general SSE decomposition. Panel B uses the same four observations as Figure 4.2: the reduced fit is (3, 3, 3, 3), the blue diagonal is labeled SST = 8, the green side SSR = 7.2, and the orange side SSE = 0.8. All side labels are squared lengths. The bottom identity reads 8 = 7.2 + 0.8."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-pos: "H"
source("illustrations/anova-sums-and-geometry.R")
draw_nested_ss_geometry(y, yhat)
```

### Why subtract the two residual sums of squares? {.unnumbered}

::: {.proof}

Fit nested OLS models to the same response vector and observations. Write $\mathbf P_R$ and $\mathbf P_F$ for the orthogonal projections onto their mean spaces, so

$$
\hat{\mathbf Y}_R=\mathbf P_R\mathbf Y,\qquad
\hat{\mathbf Y}_F=\mathbf P_F\mathbf Y,\qquad
\mathbf e_R=\mathbf Y-\hat{\mathbf Y}_R,\qquad
\mathbf e_F=\mathbf Y-\hat{\mathbf Y}_F.
$$

The reduced-model residual splits into two parts:

$$
\underbrace{\mathbf Y-\hat{\mathbf Y}_R}_{\mathbf e_R}
=
\underbrace{\hat{\mathbf Y}_F-\hat{\mathbf Y}_R}_{\text{change in fitted values}}
+
\underbrace{\mathbf Y-\hat{\mathbf Y}_F}_{\mathbf e_F}.
$$

Both fitted vectors belong to the full-model space. Their difference therefore lies in that space and is orthogonal to $\mathbf e_F$. Taking squared lengths gives

$$
\mathrm{SSE}_R
=\|\hat{\mathbf Y}_F-\hat{\mathbf Y}_R\|^2+\mathrm{SSE}_F,
$$

and hence

$$
\boxed{\mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_F
=\|\hat{\mathbf Y}_F-\hat{\mathbf Y}_R\|^2
=\mathbf Y^\top(\mathbf P_F-\mathbf P_R)\mathbf Y.}
$$

:::

The difference is nonnegative and measures the part of the reduced-model residual that the full model can fit. This identity requires nested OLS fits on the same observations; normal errors and an intercept are not needed.

### Recovering Theorem 4.2 from Theorem 4.3 {.unnumbered}

::: {.proof}

Now choose the reduced model to be **intercept only**, with rank $p_R=1$. Its fitted value for every observation is $\bar Y$, so

$$
\hat{\mathbf Y}_R=\bar Y\,\mathbf1_n,\qquad
\mathrm{SSE}_R=\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y)^2=\mathrm{SST}.
$$

Let the full model contain an intercept and have rank $p_F=p$. Then

$$
\mathrm{SSE}_F=\mathrm{SSE},\qquad
\mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_F
=\mathrm{SST}-\mathrm{SSE}
=\mathrm{SSR},\qquad
p_F-p_R=p-1.
$$

Substituting these quantities into @thm-partial-f gives exactly @thm-overall-f:

$$
\underbrace{\frac{(\mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_F)/(p_F-p_R)}
{\mathrm{SSE}_F/(n-p_F)}}_{\text{partial F statistic}}
=
\underbrace{\frac{\mathrm{SSR}/(p-1)}{\mathrm{SSE}/(n-p)}}_{\text{overall F statistic}}.
$$

The null hypothesis also becomes the overall null: the full-model mean is constant, or equivalently, all its non-intercept coefficients are zero.

:::

For the four observations in @fig-anova-variation, the intercept-only fit has $\mathrm{SSE}_R=8.0$, and the fitted line has $\mathrm{SSE}_F=0.8$. Thus

$$
F=\frac{(8.0-0.8)/(2-1)}{0.8/(4-2)}
=\frac{7.2}{0.4}=18,
$$

which is the same calculation as $\mathrm{MSR}/\mathrm{MSE}$ in @exm-anova-by-hand.

::: {.callout-note title="When the reduced model already has predictors"}

If both models contain an intercept, they share the same centered $\mathrm{SST}$. Therefore

$$
\mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_F
=(\mathrm{SST}-\mathrm{SSR}_R)-(\mathrm{SST}-\mathrm{SSR}_F)
=\mathrm{SSR}_F-\mathrm{SSR}_R.
$$

The numerator uses the **additional** explained variation beyond the reduced model. It is generally not the full model's entire $\mathrm{SSR}_F$. For example, adding height to diameter explains about $524.30-421.92=102.38$ additional squared-volume units; the variation already explained by diameter is excluded.

:::

### Why does the ratio have an F distribution? {.unnumbered}

::: {.proof}

Let $q=p_F-p_R$ and assume the normal, common-variance model in @thm-partial-f. Under $H_0$, the mean vector $\boldsymbol\mu$ lies in the reduced-model space. Nestedness implies

$$
\mathbf P_F\mathbf P_R=\mathbf P_R\mathbf P_F=\mathbf P_R.
$$

Consequently, $\mathbf A=\mathbf P_F-\mathbf P_R$ and $\mathbf B=\mathbf I-\mathbf P_F$ are symmetric idempotent matrices of ranks $q$ and $n-p_F$. Also, $\mathbf A\mathbf B=\mathbf0$, $\mathbf A\boldsymbol\mu=\mathbf0$, and $\mathbf B\boldsymbol\mu=\mathbf0$. The normal projection results from [Chapter 3](03_OLS_inference.qmd) therefore give

$$
\frac{\mathrm{SSE}_R-\mathrm{SSE}_F}{\sigma^2}
=\frac{\mathbf Y^\top\mathbf A\mathbf Y}{\sigma^2}
\sim\chi^2_q,\qquad
\frac{\mathrm{SSE}_F}{\sigma^2}
=\frac{\mathbf Y^\top\mathbf B\mathbf Y}{\sigma^2}
\sim\chi^2_{n-p_F},
$$

independently. Their ratio, after dividing each by its degrees of freedom, has distribution $F_{q,n-p_F}$.

:::

Under $H_0$, both mean squares estimate $\sigma^2$. The full-model residual provides an independent noise estimate; $\mathrm{SSE}_R$ includes the improvement being tested. The geometric identity alone does not establish the F distribution: normal, common-variance errors are also required.
